Package hadur2.core.model

Class Wave

java.lang.Object
hadur2.core.model.Wave
All Implemented Interfaces:
Cloneable
public class Wave extends Object implements Cloneable
A wave: the circle a bullet fired at fireTime from sourceLocation would lie on, growing by bulletSpeed() pixels every tick. Whatever angle the shooter chose, its bullet is somewhere on that circle, so when the circle sweeps past the target the angle that would have hit can be measured and learned from, without knowing where the real bullet went.

The duel makes two waves at every scan. A gun wave goes from us at the enemy, and the gun learns from where the enemy was when it broke; it is a firingWave only if we really fired on that tick. A movement wave goes from the enemy at us, and becomes a firing wave when the energy ledger finds that the enemy fired on its tick (WAVE-1, WAVE-2); only those are surfed. WaveManager holds them and decides when each one breaks.

Guess factors. Angles on a wave are measured from absBearing, the bearing from source to target at fire time, and scaled by the most the target could have moved off that line before the bullet arrived. A guess factor of 0 is head-on; 1 is the full escape angle in the target's orbitDirection (the way it was moving round the source), -1 the full escape angle the other way. Scaling by the escape angle, and mirroring by the orbit direction, lets what was learned at one distance, bullet power and direction of travel apply to another. The classic scale is maxEscapeAngle(), asin(8 / bulletSpeed): a robot at most 8 px/tick fast, moving square to the line of fire, against a bullet of that speed. The precise scale, preciseEscapeAngle(boolean), simulates the target's escape on each side and accounts for the walls.

Engine facts relied on. A bullet of power p moves at 20 - 3p px/tick. Robots are 36 by 36 pixel squares aligned with the axes. Each turn the engine moves every bullet before any robot, so a bullet's move from radius r(t) to r(t + 1) is tested against where the robot stood at the end of tick t; that is why checkWavePosition(hadur2.core.model.RobotState) and preciseIntersection(java.util.List<hadur2.core.model.RobotState>) test a state of tick t against the next tick's radius.

Bullet shadows (MOVE-1). A wave from the enemy also carries the firing angles at which its bullet would meet one of ours in flight and never arrive; the movement computes them (move.BulletShadows) and scales the danger at each angle by what is left unshadowed (shadowedFraction(hadur2.core.model.Wave.Intersection)).

The target attributes (target... fields) are a snapshot of the target at fire time. They are the raw features the KNN formulas in the gun and movement packages turn into search coordinates. Angles are absolute radians (0 = north, clockwise); note that absBearing comes from atan2 and may be negative. Distances are pixels, times ticks. The fields are public and mutable, as in the 1.20 code this was ported from.

    • transmission

      public List<double[]> transmission(Wave.Intersection intersection)
      MOVE-3: how much of a bullet fired at each angle of the intersection would still reach us. The range angle +/- bandwidth is cut at every shadow edge into segments {from, to, transmission}: 0 inside a certain shadow, 0.5 where the shadow is only possible (a bullet stopped about half the time), 1 elsewhere. The segments are in ascending order and cover the whole range; with no shadows it is one segment at 1.
      Parameters:
      intersection - the firing angles that would hit us
      Returns:
      the segments, never empty for a positive width

    • inShadow

      public boolean inShadow(double angle, double tolerance)
      MOVE-1: whether a bullet fired along angle from the source may meet one of ours. The core uses it as a self-check: an enemy bullet our bullet destroyed should have been fired inside a possible shadow.
      Parameters:
      angle - the firing angle, absolute radians
      tolerance - radians of slack on each side of every shadow
      Returns:
      whether the angle lies in a possible shadow, within the tolerance

    • virtuality

      public double virtuality()
      Gun waves: how far this wave is, in time, from a real bullet, in units of 8 ticks. A firing wave is 0. Otherwise it is the smaller of the ticks since our last real bullet and the ticks until the gun is cool again, over 8; before the round's first bullet, only the second counts and the result is capped at 1. The gun's KNN formulas use it as one dimension (the query while aiming uses 0), so virtual waves close in time to a real shot sit near the real ones.

A movement wave's values are recomputed when MoveController.updateFiringWave corrects its power (WAVE-4).

    • displacementVector

      public Point2D.Double displacementVector(Point2D.Double botLocation, long time)
      The target's movement from its fire-time location to botLocation, reached at time, in a frame that makes it comparable across situations: the direction is taken relative to the target's direction of travel at fire time and mirrored by the orbit direction, and the length is divided by the ticks elapsed, giving pixels per tick. Replayed with projectLocationBlind(java.awt.geom.Point2D.Double, java.awt.geom.Point2D.Double, long), it gives where the same movement would take the target from another wave's situation, walls included. time must be after the fire time.
      Parameters:
      botLocation - where the target was, pixels
      time - the tick it was there
      Returns:
      the vector, x to the side and y along the direction of travel, px per tick

    • projectLocationFromDisplacementVector

      public Point2D.Double projectLocationFromDisplacementVector(Point2D.Double dispVector)
      Where dispVector would take this wave's target if a bullet were fired from the source at fire time, by the same fixed-point replay as projectLocationBlind(java.awt.geom.Point2D.Double, java.awt.geom.Point2D.Double, long) with no extra ticks.

    • projectLocationBlind

      public Point2D.Double projectLocationBlind(Point2D.Double myNextLocation, Point2D.Double dispVector, long currentTime)
      Where dispVector would take this wave's target by the time a bullet fired now, from myNextLocation, reaches it. "Blind" because it starts from the wave's fire-time snapshot, not from a newer scan: the target has been moving along the vector since the fire time, so the ticks from then until the bullet leaves the gun (currentTime - fireTime + 1) are added to the flight time. The guns aim at the bearing of the result.
      Parameters:
      myNextLocation - where our gun will be when the bullet is fired, pixels
      dispVector - a displacement vector from displacementVector(hadur2.core.model.RobotState)
      currentTime - the current tick
      Returns:
      the projected target location, pixels (not clipped to the field)

    • projectLocation

      Point2D.Double projectLocation(Point2D.Double firingLocation, Point2D.Double dispVector, long extraTicks)
      Replays a displacement vector from the target's fire-time location. The target is taken to move along the vector's direction (turned back from the wave's frame into an absolute angle) at the vector's length per tick, for the bullet's flight time from firingLocation plus extraTicks. The flight time depends on where the target ends up, which depends on the flight time, so the two are iterated to a fixed point.
      Parameters:
      firingLocation - where the bullet is fired from, pixels
      dispVector - a displacement vector in this wave's frame
      extraTicks - ticks of movement before the bullet is in flight
      Returns:
      the projected target location, pixels

    • checkWavePosition

      public Wave.WavePosition checkWavePosition(RobotState currentState, boolean skipMidair, Wave.WavePosition maxPosition)
      Where this wave is relative to a robot in currentState, judged by the bullet's next move: from the radius at currentState.time to the radius a tick later, which the engine tests against the robot's box as it stands in that state (bullets move before robots).
      • Wave.WavePosition.MIDAIR: the next move ends short of the robot's box.
      • Wave.WavePosition.BREAKING_FRONT: it reaches the box but not the centre.
      • Wave.WavePosition.BREAKING_CENTER: it passes the centre, but the wave has not yet passed every corner.
      • Wave.WavePosition.GONE: the wave already encloses the whole box, so its bullet can no longer touch the robot.
      Parameters:
      currentState - the robot's state; its tick sets the radii
      skipMidair - whether to skip the mid-air test, when the caller knows the wave has arrived
      maxPosition - the furthest position to test for, or null for all: the result is the actual position or this one, whichever comes first, and tests beyond it are skipped
      Returns:
      the position

    • preciseIntersection

      public Wave.Intersection preciseIntersection(List<RobotState> waveBreakStates)
      The range of firing angles whose bullet would have touched the robot, given its states on the ticks this wave was crossing it: the precise intersection.

      On each such tick the bullet moves along a short segment of its ray, between the radius at that tick and the radius a tick later, and the engine tests that segment against the robot's box. So the angles that hit are those of the points of the box lying in the ring between those two radii. That region's extreme angles are always among: the box's corners inside the ring, and the points where the box's sides cross either circle. The result spans the smallest and largest of those angles over all the ticks. The virtual guns score against it, and the surf uses it both to log where the enemy aimed and as the width of the angles a candidate position would be hit by.

      Parameters:
      waveBreakStates - the robot's states on the ticks the wave was crossing it (from WaveManager or the surf's prediction), in any order
      Returns:
      the centre angle and half-width, or null when there are no states or no angle hits
